Mr. Speaker, with your leave, and especially to come to the defence of the Chair, I feel obliged to explain to my opposition friends that I was not personally informed of the fact that the people whose presence I mentioned a few minutes ago in our gallery would, in fact, be visiting the House. Like most members here in the House, when these people entered the gallery, I was surprised to see them, and I decided to take the initiative of rising on a point of order, after Question Period, to draw the attention of the House to their presence.
What I wish to say to hon. members, through you, Mr. Speaker, is that the Chair was not involved at all in this initiative taken by the Deputy House Leader. I want it to be quite clear that this decision, which I made personally, was well beyond any control the Chair might have.
So I want to make it quite clear to all members of this House that the person chairing the proceedings of this House today was not involved at all in the decision I made to draw the attention of the House to the presence of our visitors.
That being said, Mr. Speaker, I think we should also realize that from time to time, there may be situations when members of this House may decide to draw attention to the presence of distinguished citizens who
Points of Order
may be in our galleries unannounced, and that from time to time we should offer some leeway to those who take this kind of initiative. I believe that is the case today.
So as far as I am concerned, Mr. Speaker, and in concluding, I would like to say that if you decide to give me a reprimand because I drew the attention of the House to the presence of Messrs. Howe, Shack, Worsely and Maurice "Rocket" Richard in our gallery today, I accept that reprimand with great pleasure.

Mr. Speaker, I will not let this go by that easily. I think the hon. minister totally misrepresented what we are trying to do. I did not blame the Speaker and that was not our intention. We said it is a custom be informed, and the minister is trying to sidetrack the debate. Of course the Speaker is not going to blame the minister today, and I know the minister would like to say he was blamed for recognizing great people that we all want to applaud. That is not the point.
The point raised by my esteemed colleague from Toronto is that it has always been our practice, in order not to have this kind of debate, for Mr. Speaker to recognize visitors, hon. minister, the next time such an occasion arises, he can take a pen, and if he needs one I can lend him mine any time, to send a little distinguished note to Mr. Speaker saying, "Mr. Speaker, I see in the gallery distinguished people who should be recognized." Then Mr. Speaker will do so.

Mr. Speaker, I think you have to be very careful here. I too along with all members of the House appreciated the minister so gallantly rising and pointing out some very distinguished guests. We all felt that was an appropriate act.
However, if this becomes any kind of open season, we all have distinguished guests to which we might draw attention. I observe, Mr. Speaker, that you have been very liberal in your efforts in the last while to recognize the people in our gallery, recognizing that that time comes out of Question Period, which is the only time we have to hold the government accountable. That can be problematic. On the other hand, I am sure others have noticed that you use the occasion from time to time to defuse the House when it perhaps becomes a little too

November 28, 1989
Points of Order
rambunctious, by focusing our attention on esteemed guests in the gallery.
I think it is important that we all have a clear understanding that it is the Speaker who recognizes guests on our behalf, because if we turn this into an open season situation, we will all be up on points of order at the end of Question Period pointing out various guests. I think that my hon. friend knows the rules and regulations and I simply would ask him, and not only his colleagues but all of us, to recognize the time honoured tradition that it is the Speaker who recognizes guests in the gallery on behalf of us all.

speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
speechtext:
This may be the appropriate time for some comments by the Chair. I want to thank the Hon. Member for Saint-Denis and the minister for their comments, especially the hon. member for Saint-Denis, since he is an expert on the rules of the House of Commons and one of our veteran members. I listened carefully to the comments made by the hon. member, wise as always.
I believe the comments made by the Hon. Member for Parkdale-High Park were particularly apt.

Let me just point out to hon. members that after the House joined together in a happy demonstration of felicity and welcome to the distinguished visitors in the gallery, I pointed out that the entire procedure was, of course, highly out of order. I might have likened the situation to a hockey game, but I resisted that temptation. I can only say to the hon. member for Parkdale- High Park that under the circumstances I could not put all hon. members on both sides of the House in the penalty box.
But we have a procedure which I think ought to be followed, that is, that first of all there are some guidelines with regard to whom we recognize. The proper procedure is that at some time well in advance of the moment when the guests are expected notice is given to the Speaker.
I am always in the hands of hon. members. If the House wants, by consent, to change that on some special
occasion, of course the House can do so. I think the consent that we saw this afternoon was one that sort of crept around the chamber and nobody, under the circumstances, wished to be other than gracious. I understand that.
The difficulty we have, though, is: as the hon. member for Kamloops pointed out, all hon. members have people of great distinction living in their ridings. After all, without the support of these people of great distinction, hon. members would not be here. There is a natural tendency and natural temptation to want to recognize these people. Sometimes the distinction they have as great Canadians has a great deal to do with how close they live to the hon. member back in the riding. But that is not a matter for me to concern myself with as long as the suggestion for recognition meets the guidelines. The guidelines are veiy clear and hon. members have them.
I would say to the hon. minister that I think there was some complicity on both sides of the House with the hon. minister's very generous use of a moment or two after Question Period. I want to assure the hon. minister that I am not taking any of these remarks as any kind of an attack on the Chair. I just want to advise hon. members and the public, of course, that I do not think this was quite the individual initiative that the minister may have indicated to the House it was, because an hon. member from this side of the House had come to me and said: "When are we going to recognize these special guests?"
This is one of those rare moments when the House expressed its unanimous wish to do something, but I think I should say that it is a rare moment and, unless I am advised differently by the House, I am going to stick to the rules and recognitions will not be made unless I have notice and unless they fit the guidelines.

Mr. Speaker, I heard the comments of the parliamentary secretary on the point that I raised, and I am quite happy to accept his statement of apology. On that basis I would gladly withdraw my point of order.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to table, in both official languages, a number of Order in Council appointments which were made by the government.
Of course all this is pursuant to Section 110(1).

subtopic: ELECTIONS, PRIVILEGES, PROCEDURE AND PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS TABLING OF REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE

speakeroldname: Mr. Peter Milliken (Kingston and the Islands):
subtopic: ELECTIONS, PRIVILEGES, PROCEDURE AND PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS TABLING OF REPORT OF STANDING COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have the honour to table in the House the Sixth Report of the Standing Committee on Elections, Privileges, Procedure and Private Members' Business. The Committee has designated a motion as a votable item, and it is motion No. 524, standing in the name of the Hon. Member for Scarborough Centre.
[Editor's note: See today's Votes and Proceedings.]

Mr. Speaker, it is my delight to present a petition, pursuant to Standing Order
Routine Proceedings
36, on behalf of a number of people from British Columbia who point out their concern for the government's goods and services tax.
While pointing out most of the shortcomings of the tax, the petitioners simply ask the government to reconsider proceeding, to go back to the drawing board and to start all over again.

Mr. Speaker, on a second item, again pursuant to Standing Order 36 and certified correct by the clerk of petitions, I wish to present a petition from 72 western Canadians who point out the need for the government to reconsider its decision on VIA Rail cut-backs and actually upgrade VIA Rail with new equipment and give VIA Rail a sufficient budget to maintain its national mandate for passenger service.

Mr. Speaker, I rise pursuant to Standing Order 36 with three petitions, two of them with a total of 101 signatures, asking the government not to make any cuts on VIA Rail and to wait until a new transportation policy can be brought into effect.
Mr. Speaker, I have a third petition on a totally unrelated matter from many persons in my constituency from the cities of Brantford, Paris, Ontario and so on who are completely opposed to abortion.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, pursuant to Standing Order 36, it is my duty and obligation to present three separate groups of petitions to the House today, all of which have been certified correct as to form and content by the clerk.
First, some 37 signatories from my riding of Sarnia- Lambton call upon the Parliament of Canada to urge the Governor in Council to exercise his constitutional power of disallowance with respect to Bill 178 of the province of Quebec which they believe contravenes the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms.

speechtext:

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Labour
speechtext: Finally, Mr. Speaker, I have received some 4,400 signatures from residents of Sarnia, Clearwater, Brights Grove, Point Edward, Corunna, Courtright and other communities throughout Ontario who humbly pray and call upon Parliament to pass legislation which establishes mandatory minimum sentences for all violent crimes that would apply uniformly to all regions of Canada.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Agriculture); Parliamentary Secretary to the Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is my honour as a member of Parliament to present several petitions from constituents in the lower mainland, but also from Vancouver Island. The list comprises several hundred names and their petition reads as follows:
The undersigned humbly pray and call upon Parliament to preserve the distinctive heritage and tradition of the RCMP by retaining uniformity of dress code with all the recognizable colour and trappings that have such great historical value for this country.
The pride and esprit de corps should not be jeopardized by any concession to religious or ethnic minorities which result in changes to this truly great police force and its proud traditions and uniform.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of State (Agriculture); Parliamentary Secretary to the Solicitor General of Canada
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have another petition of several pages on an entirely different subject which reads as follows:
The undersigned, your petitioners, humbly pray and call upon Parliament to enact legislation which will effectively protect the life of the unborn without distinction as to stage of development.

Mr. Speaker, I have the honour and duty, pursuant to Standing Order 36, to present to the House 10 petitions certified correct by the clerk of petitions.
They contain the signatures of hundreds of constituents in my riding of Hamilton West and surrounding ridings. They call on this Parliament to reject the proposed 9 per cent goods and services tax.

Mr. Speaker, I wish to present a petition with some 51 names from Kincardine, Ontario, calling on the Parliament of Canada to restore VIA Rail service, to maintain it at its present level, to upgrade the rail service with new equipment, and to give VIA Rail sufficient budget to maintain its national mandate for passenger service.

Mr. Speaker, for I do not know how many times I have done this now, but I am presenting again today a large number of petitions from people in my riding and adjacent ridings who are totally opposed to the proposed goods and services tax.
They are extremely worried about the effects this tax will have on inflation and on the cost of living. They humbly beg this Conservative government to withdraw its proposal.

Mr. Speaker, it gives me a great deal of pleasure today to present a petition from 1,320 residents of Osoyoos and district in the riding of Okanagan-Similkameen-Merritt with respect to a proposed storage site for PCBs at the port of entry of Osoyoos in the province of British Columbia. They say that this is inappropriate for an area such as Osoyoos which depends on agriculture and tourism for its economic survival.
They humbly pray and call upon Parliament to ensure that the environment of the Okanagan is not jeopardized by the potential for contamination by PCBs from such a storage site and ask the government to reconsider and reverse the decision by Public Works Canada to store PCBs at the port of entry in Osoyoos, British Columbia.

Mr. Speaker, it is my honour and privilege today to present to this House four petitions, all of which deal with the subject of the proposed goods and services tax.
No doubt it will come as no surprise that the citizens of my riding who have signed these petitions humbly pray that Parliament scrap the tax.
November 28, 1989

Mr. Speaker, pursuant to Standing Order 36, it is my duty and honour to present this petition signed by 41 petitioners. It has been certified by the clerk of petitions.
The petitioners say that the railway passenger service carried on by VIA Rail is an essential means of transportation for many Canadians and has been part of the basic Canadian infrastructure for over 100 years and that these cuts in subsidy to VIA Rail will result in serious reduction in railway passenger service.
Therefore the undersigned call upon Parliament to maintain VIA Rail, Canada's present national network; to upgrade VIA Rail with new equipment; and to give VIA Rail a sufficient budget to maintain its national mandate for passenger service.

Mr. Speaker, I rise today to present two petitions. The first one is with respect to VIA Rail.
I have a petition with 32 names on it of Canadians who are concerned with the direction the government is taking with respect to VIA Rail.
They call upon the government to maintain VIA Rail's present national network, to upgrade VIA Rail with new equipment, and to give VIA Rail a sufficient budget to maintain its national mandate for passenger service.

Mr. Speaker, I also have another petition which has been presented to me by a number of producers in Saskatchewan who are concerned about the direction this government is taking with respect to agriculture in this country.
Specifically they are concerned about oats being removed from the jurisdiction of the Canadian Wheat Board, and they call upon this government to reinstate oats under the Wheat Board Act and to give barley the same protection that wheat has now.

Mr. Speaker, it is my privilege to present another petition on behalf of my Cardigan constituents, particularly from the Souris area.
Routine Proceedings
The petitioners pray that this government will bring forth legislation that will protect the foetus.

Mr. Speaker, I have three sets of petitions to table this afternoon. The petitions have all been certified correct as to form and content by the clerk of petitions.
I would like to table a petition signed by approximately 97 residents of Toronto, Sault Ste. Marie and Beard-more, one from Scotland and two from New York City, who are concerned about the decisions of the government with regard to VIA Rail.
They point out that these reductions in budget and service will lead to the disappearance of one-third of Canada's national railway system, if not more. They call upon Parliament to upgrade VIA Rail with new equipment and to give VIA Rail a sufficient budget to maintain its national mandate for passenger service.

Mr. Speaker, I have the honour to table in the House today petitions bearing the names of approximately 16,000 Canadians who work in and around the Great Lakes-St. Lawrence Seaway system.
They point out in this petition that the federal government has failed to establish a national marine policy and that that in itself has contributed to the reflagging of Canadian ships and offered Canadian shipping companies a loophole whereby they do not pay taxes.
The petitioners point out that this reflagging has cost Canadians thousands of jobs, both directly and indirectly, on board ships and in the related shore-side and ship building industries, and that this has a dramatic impact on the communities as well as the federal Treasury.
The petitioners call on Parliament to endorse the concept of a Canadian international shipping registry, also known as a second registry, for Canadian ships operating in international trade outside Canada as detailed in the discussion paper prepared by Transport Canada dated September 1988.

November 28, 1989
Routine Proceedings PROPOSED GOODS AND SERVICES TAX

Mr. Speaker, I also have a number of petitions with regard to the goods and services tax signed by citizens in my community who object to the proposed tax, whether it is 9, 8, 7, 6, or 5 per cent.
Some 71 customers of Wheeler's Lumber have petitioned me, as well as 26 from G. K. Sandwich Take-Out and 26 from McMillan Grocery. I would like to table those.

speakeroldname: Mr. Albert Cooper (Parliamentary Secretary to Government House Leader):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada; Parliamentary Secretary to the Leader of the Government in the House of Commons
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the following questions will be answered today: Nos. 151 and 157.

Has the government planned celebrations in 1992 for the one hundred and twenty-fifth anniversary of Confederation and, if so, in this regard, has the government (a) issued contracts to plan or help organize the events and, if so (i) what number (ii) for what amounts (b) set a budget and, if so, for what amount (c) assigned duties to departmental staff and, if so, by department, to what number of them (d) prepared a list of themes or possible events and, if so, what are they (e) prepared a study of funding provided to projects in the 1967 Centennial year and, if so, what is its title?

speakeroldname: Hon. Gerry Weiner (Secretary of State of Canada and Minister of State (Multiculturalism and Citizenship)):
speakerposition: Secretary of State of Canada; Minister of State (Multiculturalism and Citizenship)
speechtext:
No, see footnote.
A national conference, entitled "Towards 1992", which was held in Ottawa from October 10 to 12, brought together some 400 representatives from all sectors of Canadian society including the private sector. The objective was to determine how best to co-ordinate efforts in commemorating a number of significant anniversaries
being marked across the country, in 1992, including the 125th anniversary of Canadian Confederation.

Has the Dundee Resort been sold by Enterprise Cape Breton
Corporation and, if so (a) to whom (b) for what amount (c) what
conditions were attached to the sale (d) who were the alternative
bidders?

speakeroldname: Hon. Elmer Macintosh MacKay (Minister of Public Works and Minister for the purposes of the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency Act):
speakerposition: Minister for the purposes of the Atlantic Canada Opportunities Agency Act; Minister of Public Works
speechtext:
In August 1987, the Cape Breton Development Corporation called proposals for the possible sale and future development of Dundee Resort. The Corporation received (5) requests for information and (3) proposals for development, from 1) Dundee Development Limited; 2) South Mountain Arm of Gold Community Association; and 3) Odyssey Cape Breton Limited. The Odyssey Cape Breton Limited concept was selected as the most promising project for consideration.
Dundee Resort has not yet been sold. Dundee's Board of Directors and ECBC's Board of Directors have approved the sale of Dundee Resort subject to satisfactory completion of negotiations with Odyssey Cape Breton Limited.
